--- title: "Benin Malaria Epidemiology Summary" format: html --- ## 1. Introduction Benin is a narrow, elongated country in West Africa bordered by Togo, Burkina Faso, Niger, and Nigeria, with a population of roughly 14.5 million (WHO, 2023; World Bank, 2024). Malaria is endemic nationally and remains the leading cause of under-five mortality and a significant cause of adult morbidity, placing Benin among the 15 highest-burden countries globally (WHO World Malaria Report, 2024). This profile consolidates the country's administrative and demographic context, malaria epidemiology, control history, and health system to support evidence-based planning and correct interpretation of MAP's model outputs. --- ## 2. Summary Statistics Country and malaria summary indicators are compiled from the World Malaria Report/WHO Global Health Observatory, HMIS/DHIS2 reporting, and the MIS 2022 survey. Where WHO's modelled estimates diverge substantially from routine-reported figures, both are shown, since this distinction matters for correct interpretation of burden. ````` ::: ::: --- ## 3. Administrative Boundaries Benin comprises 12 departments, subdivided into 77 communes, further divided into 546 arrondissements, composed of 5,295 villages. The health system, however, is organized around 34 health zones, which do not correspond one-to-one with communes or departments (PMI, 2023), a distinction worth flagging for any stratification or spatial analysis intended to align with programmatic decision-making, since correspondence between department/commune boundaries and health-zone boundaries will need to be resolved before model outputs from this profile can be used at the health-zone level. **Figure:** Benin_StudyArea_Map **Caption:** Administrative departments of Benin, showing the 12 departments and their capitals as well as the number of communes per department, the capital (Porto-Novo, blue), and main city (Cotonou, red) ::: {.det-source} **Source:** Institut géographique National du Bénin (IGN-Benin) via Humanitarian Data Exchange, 2026 ::: --- ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Administrative geography of Benin: 12 departments and 34 communes.](benin_files/figure-html/fig-admin-map-1.png){#fig-admin-map width=864} ::: ::: **Source:** Administrative boundaries: Malaria Atlas Project (release 202403), retrieved 2026-10-21. ## 4. Malaria Situation Three transmission zones are recognized nationally: a heterogeneous southern coastal zone, a holoendemic central plateau, and a markedly seasonal northern Sahelian zone, with *Plasmodium falciparum* responsible for 98-100% of infections (PMI, 2023; WHO, 2024). Benin is among the 15 highest-burden countries globally, accounting for an estimated 2% of global malaria cases and 1.7% of global malaria deaths in 2023 (Severe Malaria Observatory, 2024). Malaria remains the leading cause of under-five mortality and accounts for roughly 37–40% of outpatient consultations and 25% of hospital admissions nationally (PMI, 2018). Routine surveillance shows a rising absolute caseload alongside a declining test positivity rate over 2018-2022, consistent with expanding diagnostic access rather than worsening transmission. --- ## 5. History of Malaria (last 20 years) Benin's malaria response built out steadily from the mid-2000s: ACTs became first-line treatment in 2004, free LLINs and IPTp were adopted in 2008, and a nationwide mass LLIN campaign followed in 2011 alongside free case management for children under five and pregnant women. IRS was rolled out in phases - Ouémé (2008), expanding south (2010) and north to Atacora (2011) - while the National Malaria Strategic Plan 2017-2021 set the long-term goal of malaria being “no longer a public health problem” by 2030. Seasonal malaria chemoprevention was introduced in 2019 and expanded through 2021, reflecting growing recognition of the seasonal transmission pattern in the north. National parasite prevalence (RDT, children 6-59 months) moved from 25% (2011-12) to 37% (2015), 36% (2017-18), and 32% (2022). The RTS,S malaria vaccine was rolled out in 2024, the most recent addition to the prevention package (Alohoutade et al., 2026). **Figure:** Benin_history_timeline **Caption:** History of malaria control in Benin, 2004–2024, with national parasite prevalence (RDT, children 6–59 months) ::: {.det-source} **Source:** Compiled from PMI Benin Malaria Profile; DHS/MIS survey rounds (see References) ::: --- ## 6. Health System Benin's health system follows a three-tier pyramidal structure: central (Ministry of Health, national hospitals), intermediate (12 departments, via Departmental Health Directorates), and peripheral (34 health zones, via Health Zone Management Teams). Each reports through DHIS2, with paper forms still used peripherally (PMI, 2023). Community health workers (relais communautaires for prevention/referral, agents de santé communautaires qualifiés for testing/treatment) support the peripheral tier, though only 36 of roughly 1,474 CHWs nationally currently provide malaria testing services. Facility coverage rose from 89% (2005) to 96% (2021), financing runs through a common-basket system with free case management for the highest-risk groups, and DHIS2 reporting completeness reached 99.5% by 2022. **Figure:** benin_health_pyramid **Caption:** Benin health system reporting structure. ::: {.det-source} **Source:** U.S. President's Malaria Initiative (2023). Benin Malaria Profile, PMI FY2024 (see references) ::: --- ## 8. Stratification Maps / SNT Benin's stratification has evolved from the coarse MARA/ARMA national risk map, through the NMSP 2017-2021's three-zone ecological classification, to the 2021 PNLP/Swiss TPH health-zone-level modelling exercise that directly informed Benin's 2021–2023 Global Fund funding request. The most recent publicly available products are the MARA/ARMA-updated transmission-season map and the MIS 2022 department-level RDT prevalence maps for pregnant women and children under five. Benin is not among the original 10 WHO HBHI countries that underwent the standardized SNT process, so these remain the most current stratification outputs identified for this profile. **Figure:** benin_stratification1 **Caption:** Start month of the malaria transmission season by department ::: {.det-source} **Source:** MARA/ARMA, updated with 2021 case data ::: **Figure:** benin_stratification2 **Caption:** Malaria prevalence (RDT) by department, MIS 2022: (1) pregnant women, (2) children under 5 ::: {.det-source} **Source:** U.S. President's Malaria Initiative ::: --- ## 9. Environment and Seasonality Malaria transmission tracks Benin's north-south climatic gradient: a sub-equatorial, bimodal-rainfall south (transmission starting April), a transitional central plateau (June), and a semi-arid Sahelian north with a single rainy season (July) (MARA/ARMA, 2021). Nationally, peak transmission spans April–October, but this masks the zonal heterogeneity that determines, for example, SMC eligibility in the north, which requires at least 60% of annual cases to fall within a 4-month window (Merle et al., 2023). The Harmattan dry-season wind further suppresses vector breeding and marks the national low-transmission window. --- ## 10. Vector Profile *Plasmodium falciparum* causes 98-100% of infections in Benin, transmitted primarily by the *Anopheles gambiae* complex: *An. coluzzii* (~91%), *An. gambiae* s.s. (~8%), and hybrids (~1%), with *An. funestus* as a secondary vector and *An. arabiensis*/*An. nili* also present (PMI, 2023; WHO, 2024). Insecticide resistance is now the central operational constraint: pyrethroid resistance is confirmed at 100% of sites tested, partially restored by PBO synergist, while carbamate resistance is present at 57% of sites, and organophosphate, pirimiphos-methyl, and chlorfenapyr susceptibility remain intact. IRS was phased in from 2008 to 2011 but PMI funding ended in 2021, and the Centre de Recherche Entomologique de Cotonou (CREC) remains the primary source for more granular vector data. **Figure (maps recommended):** benin_vector_dry_vs_rainy **Caption:** Dominant malaria vector species by department in Benin: (1) dry season, (2) rainy season. *An. coluzzii* predominates nationally in the dry season and in the south year-round; *An. gambiae* becomes more represented in parts of the north and center during the rainy season, with the exception of Malanville (Alibori), which remains couzzii-dominant in both seasons. ::: {.det-source} **Source:** Akpodji S, Agbangla C, Akogbéto M, et al.
